newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bonn, Paris challenge US on limiting NATO entries.
newsitem.headline: Bonn, Paris challenge US on limiting NATO entries.

text.p: The leaders of France and Germany defied Washington on Friday by insisting they would support bids by Romania and Slovenia to join NATO soon despite American objections.

The Western alliance tried to reassure the two jilted ex-communist applicants but gave them no concrete prospect of later entry, and both said they would not give up their bids to join NATO in its first wave of expansion.

The White House had surprised European NATO members on Thursday by telling them it was set on limiting the first wave to three central European countries -- the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland -- and did not expect to be overruled.

But French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl made clear they were not ready to let Washington declare the matter closed ahead of a July 8-9 NATO summit in Madrid, due to open the door to new members to the east.
"We will indeed support the candidacy of Romania despite the reticence expressed by the American government," Chirac told reporters after a Franco-German summit in Poitiers.
"One individual statement is in no way an advance decision," Kohl said.
"There is no doubt about the entry of three countries. There is now a discussion about whether three or five countries come into line, including Romania and Slovenia."
He said Germany wanted all five to be told in Madrid that they would be part of NATO's development.

But NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, speaking to reporters after a meeting of NATO defence ministers, offered no prospects that the summit would provide tangible consolation to countries left out of the first wave.
"My impression, my opinion is that in the communique, there will not be set a particular date, a particular moment, particular names who will be invited to a second wave."
He said the ministers stressed the door to the alliance would remain open, and NATO's partners in eastern Europe would all have more involvement in NATO headquarters in Brussels.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said before a meeting with the foreign minister of Latvia, another would-be NATO member, that "NATO will remain open to all European democracies that are able to contribute to its goals".
The reassurances seemed too little for Slovenia.
"If the door is to be open it would be good if it was to open again soon," a NATO official quoted Slovenian defence minister Turnsek Tit as saying.

Slovenian Prime Minister Janos Drnovsek said he had been surprised by the U.S. announcement and added: "Our chances for inclusion are very small but they still exist. Some NATO members said a last minute compromise was possible."
Romania, whose prime minister Victor Ciorbea is due in Washington next week to press his case, took a similar line.
"We've joined this race to win," he told reporters. "We're not going to give up now before Madrid."

A French official said the U.S. position, which went against the wishes of a majority of European NATO allies for a broader enlargement, appeared to be dictated by the higher cost and concern in Congress over the budgetary implications.

France has long argued that the admission of Romania and Slovenia would show the alliance is as concerned about security in the Balkans, the Black Sea area and the Mediterranean as it is about its northern region.

By contrast Germany, perhaps the strongest advocate of integrating its eastern neighbours in western institutions such as NATO and the European Union, only came out publicly in favour of Romania and Slovenia this week.
Hardline Romanian nationalist leader Corneliu Vadim Tudor added to fears that rejection might cause resentment, saying: "This was only to be expected. The West never really loved us."

But Drnovsek said a cold shoulder from NATO might have hidden benefits. "In world politics there are compensations... Support for Slovenia's candidacy to join the EU is likely to increase as a compensation (for the NATO decision)," he said.
